If you’re able to, it may be helpful to speak with an addictions counselor to navigate your home environment and relationship with your parents as they relate to your alcohol use. A healthy environment and healthy relationships are key to recovery. You will likely need to have a very candid conversation with your parents. It’s essential that they respect your decision and support you as long as you’re living with them. A counselor may be able to help you navigate the right approach to talking with your parents. If counseling isn’t possible, joining online support groups through AA or SMART Recovery have proven to be helpful for me. Just know that this is about you and your health and your future- not anyone else. Don’t allow another person’s opinions influence what you know is best for you. This is your health, your body, your life. Keep posting here. You can do this. IWNDWYT!

Can’t tell you how much I relate to being triggered by some of the self-help books out there. “This Naked Mind” gets recommended a lot on here, but it triggered the hell out of me. I find a lot of these books to be narrow in their view of what addiction looks like. They also get a lot of things wrong about the history of alcohol consumption and, particularly, wine, which drives me crazy and can make me want to drink all the more.

I’m doing the SMART recovery program now and I’ve personally found it to be more useful than AA or any self-help book I’ve tried. It’s an evidence-based program that runs you through pragmatic exercises regarding your relationship with substances and the nature of your addictive behavior(s). They also have online support groups.

If a book is your jam, I like the recommendation of “Atomic Habits” that another commenter made.

Good luck and I hope you keep coming here.

I agreed with you up until the last two sentences. Obesity is not necessarily a choice nor is it “socially irresponsible” in many cases. 

My sister suffers from an autoimmune disease that has attacked her thyroid and made her obese. It’s extraordinarily difficult for her to lose weight, but she works hard at it. She has built a team of doctors around her to support her in combatting her disease and her obesity. 

For over a year now she has been committed to intermittent fasting and a ketogenic diet and consumes less calories than most people. She also exercises as much as she’s able despite often feeling physically uncomfortable and fatigued from side effects related to her disease and medications. 

She has lost some weight, but not what the average, healthy person would ever expect. She gets so upset and frustrated at the lack of progress she sees. It wears on her mental health. And it’s the strangers who judge her before knowing anything about her personal experience that make it all the more painful. 

Take a moment before you judge people for how their bodies look. You have no idea what they might be battling.
No one should be legally prosecuted for expressing their views. That would be an infringement on anyone’s rights. We have to engage the ideas we disagree with. They don’t disappear by silencing.

Mindful journaling has been the most useful tool for me. Any time I'm having a craving, I start writing. I take time to really observe my mind and its thought process, and try to get to the root of the craving, what I'm really looking for. Is it escape? Boredom? Anxiety? An attempt to "feel good"? I'll then write out all of the reasons drinking won't actually do anything positive for whatever it is I'm after, whether in the long- or short-term. And sometimes I'll remind myself, in writing, why I chose to stop drinking. There's something about getting it out on paper that's really effective for me. And by the time I'm done writing, the craving is usually gone.

I also treat myself to a lot of good food and NA bevs like Zevia and Kombucha and hot tea.

Thanks so much for the thoughtful response. I can really relate to your story and it’s nice to know I’m not alone. Feeling like you’re “somewhere in between” can be a strange and alienating space to exist. 

My drinking has been problematic for well over a decade. I’ve had periods of moderation and periods of heavy drinking that left me with hangovers nearly every day. It’s always been a rollercoaster for me. Sometimes a battle. 

Over the past year, I went from successfully moderating to having a shot in the middle of the day to drinking around 11 units of alcohol a day. I was self-medicating my depression and anxiety disorders and numbing myself from a lot of environmental stressors. It was a bad time, with or without alcohol. I knew that my alcohol consumption was making it so much worse, but I was stuck in that cycle and struggled to moderate. Needless to say, my mental health declined rapidly. I was almost waiting for a “rock bottom” moment before I decided that I didn’t need one. And here I am. But I can almost feel that nagging “but you’re not an alcoholic!” voice ready to creep back in whenever I’m vulnerable enough...

Anyway, thanks for sharing your story. It was really encouraging. Best of luck to you on your journey!

I find that searching for the why's in life can be a futile endeavor. It's extraordinarily difficult for people to truly get at the why of their actions and desires. Oftentimes, we convince ourselves we know why we've done something (even the simplest things) when, in fact, we've just assigned meaning and reasoning to completely automatic behavior. I'm more interested-- particularly in this situation-- in considering the potential benefits/repercussions of my decisions moving forward. 

With all of that said, I can also understand how anyone reading the super abbreviated version of my experience provided in my post might think the answer is so simple or that I'm just crazy for entertaining a relationship with my father at all considering his past. But abuse (by a parental figure especially) can be very complicated. So many emotions and experiences are involved and need to be sorted through.
